A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Glianorex fictional-medical benchmark, with matching authors, core methodology, model panel and question examples. All 18 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including Appendices A and B, support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 14 language models on 264 fictional medical questions per language, including accuracy, statistical comparisons and per-question response distributions.

after.justification: V2 reports expanded model evaluations, physician answers and quality ratings, comparisons across question generators, and original DeepSeek prompting and interpretability analyses.

M1.justification: The fictional-textbook-to-MCQ-and-translation approach is retained. V2 extends benchmark construction with a Claude 3.5 Sonnet generation branch and physician review checkpoints before downstream generation (Section 3.1 and Figure 1). These are bounded extensions of the existing construction procedure.

E1.justification: V2 extends evaluation beyond full-question fictional MCQs to answers-only inputs and adds a cross-benchmark analysis using MedQA-USMLE scores, which v1 only discussed as background. It also evaluates Claude-generated Glianorex questions alongside GPT-generated questions. The fictional medical domain and English/French language coverage remain.

E2.justification: The original 14-model quantitative panel is retained, including Internist.ai and Meerkat under shortened names. V2 adds two physicians as an explicitly evaluated human reference on 100 English questions (Figure 2), substantially broadening the central comparison from differences among models to differences between models and medical experts.

E3.justification: V2 adds 224 Claude-generated questions per language to the 264-question GPT subsets. New protocols include physician testing without textbook exposure, randomized question order and seven-point language-quality ratings, plus four DeepSeek conditions crossing full-question versus answers-only input with direct answering versus chain-of-thought prompting (Sections 3.1.4 and 3.3; Appendix A.4).

E4.justification: V2 adds generator-dependence checks, physician audits of coherence and question quality, prompting/input ablations, an answer-length analysis, MedQA correlation analysis, and qualitative examinations of hallucinations and test-taking strategies. Conversely, v1's per-question correct-answer distribution analysis and Figure 2 are removed.

E5.justification: V1 already reports normal-approximation confidence intervals, binomial chance tests, significance comparisons and Cohen's d. V2 additionally specifies two-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD, regression inference with 95% prediction bands, and Cohen's kappa agreement analysis. It also specifies one prediction per item and ablation setting; this expands statistical reporting without establishing increased repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: The reported overall average changes from about 67% to 63.8% over an expanded question pool, so this is not a same-setting performance decline. V2 adds generator-specific scores (Table 6), physician scores of 27% each, a MedQA association with R-squared 0.5952, and DeepSeek accuracies of 70.1% for full-question zero-shot and 46.5% for answers-only zero-shot evaluation (Table 3). Effect-size and significance results are also revised.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical propositions, proofs or a formal model of the phenomenon. V2's additional standard statistical analyses do not introduce new mathematical definitions or theoretical derivations.

C1.justification: V1 centers its claims on similarly high model performance despite fictional content. V2 adds the central claim that models outperform physicians on this benchmark and explicitly attributes successful answers to shallow cues, test-taking strategies and hallucinated reasoning. Its conclusion also qualifies the earlier claim of isolating reasoning from memorization as only partial isolation.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of answers-only performance and MedQA correlation, and questions whether medical fine-tuning improves knowledge or familiarity with evaluation formats. It introduces clinician-workload concerns about reviewing reasoning traces and acknowledges bias from a single clinician's grounding material. The coherence limitation is revised following partial audits, while v1's explicit sample-size and model-selection limitations are removed.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds archival code identifiers, a standalone dataset identifier and human-annotation instructions, and reports that Glianorex tasks are available in the evaluation harness's main branch. V2 also documents vLLM, eight H200 GPUs and greedy decoding for DeepSeek, and updates the main evaluation runtime from four to ten hours. Existing generation defaults and the core evaluation command are retained.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around benchmark fragility, including MedFuzz, drug-name perturbations and medical metacognition. It connects its interpretations to work on answers-only strategies, medical adaptation and knowledge extraction, and adds literature on clinician workload and alternative clinical assessments. These additions reshape the argument beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The title changes, Related Work becomes a standalone section, and Methods and Results gain extensive hierarchical subsections. Discussion is reorganized into evaluation implications, medical implications, recommendations and alternatives; Conclusion moves before Limitations. Substantial rewriting also clarifies and shortens retained arguments.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout and adds a generation-pipeline diagram, regression plot, annotation-interface screenshot, ablation table and generator-specific results table. The accuracy figure gains a human reference, significance displays are split, and the original response-distribution figure disappears. The generation prompt and retained question examples are relocated or renumbered rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's interpretation relied mainly on high scores without reported human validation or direct input ablations. V2 adds language/coherence audits, a human reference, a second question generator and answers-only controls that substantially strengthen the evidence behind its central argument. The two-physician sample, single-model ablations and removal of explicit sample-size/model-selection caveats limit the gains, but do not outweigh the improvement in empirical support and interpretability.
